item.title: How should you pack batteries?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Nowadays, tech is everywhere when we travel, from power banks and portable fans to smart suitcases that follow their owners around the airport. But many of these devices come with a hidden risk. In October, a British Airways flight was forced to make an emergency landing after a battery fire burned one of the passengers — and this is hardly an isolated incident. The Federal Aviation Administration reported 28 battery fire events on passenger and cargo planes in the first quarter of 2026 alone. That’s on track to beat last year’s tally of 97 events, up from 89 in 2024. Fires can be particularly dangerous in the enclosed space of an airplane, so it’s critical for passengers to do their part by packing batteries correctly. Here’s an overview of the types of batteries you need to watch out for, what devices they’re in and how to pack them safely and legally. Any battery can start a fire if stored improperly, but the biggest threats are lithium metal (non-rechargeable) and lithium-ion (rechargeable) batteries. These batteries have exploded in popularity in recent years. Unfortunately, they are also at risk of, quite literally, exploding. According to the FAA, “All lithium-ion batteries are capable of overheating and experiencing a process called thermal runaway.” Thermal runaway is a self-sustaining chemical reaction that produces extreme heat (up to 1,500 degrees F within seconds), toxic smoke, ultrafine particles and flames. It can occur without warning due to various factors, including damage to the battery, overheating, overcharging, exposure to water and manufacturing defects. Lithium battery fires are often resistant to traditional extinguishing agents, making them tough for cabin crews to tackle. And since planes recirculate air rather than drawing fresh air from outside, toxic fumes from lithium fires can pose a health hazard to passengers long after the flames are extinguished. As a result, the aviation industry has been tightening the rules on lithium batteries. What devices contain lithium batteries? The most common culprits behind aircraft fires are cell phones, laptops, vapes and power banks. For example, three passengers were injured when a laptop battery caught fire on an American Airlines plane in 2024, and a power bank caused a similar emergency on a Virgin Australia flight in 2025. However, lots of other devices can contain lithium batteries, such as: - Wireless earbuds and noise-canceling headphones - Handheld gaming consoles and controllers - Wearables like smartwatches and fitness trackers - Electric toothbrushes, razors, hair curling wands and flatirons - Portable medical monitors, infusion pumps and hearing aids To determine whether your device has a lithium battery, check the label or manual. The chemical symbol “Li” generally indicates the presence of lithium; you may see terms such as "Li-polymer," "LiPo” or "Li+." For coin-cell batteries, the label will typically start with “CR” if lithium is involved. Where and how should you pack batteries? As you can see, there’s a good reason for all the restrictions around batteries on planes — but they can be confusing. If you’ve ever wondered how you should store your camera battery or whether you can pack that portable fan in your checked luggage, you’ve come to the right place. Here, I’ll answer all of your, ahem, burning questions about batteries. The regulations around lithium batteries depend on the battery size and whether they are alone or installed in a device. Non-rechargeable batteries are limited to 2 grams of lithium per battery, while rechargeable batteries are limited to a rating of 100 watt hours. According to TSA, this covers “nearly all types of lithium batteries used by the average person in their electronic devices.” Larger batteries require approval from the airline. TSA prohibits spare or uninstalled lithium batteries — which include power banks and cell phone charging cases — in checked baggage. These batteries must go in your carryon, and if you end up gate-checking your bag, you must remove them and keep them with you during the flight. For lithium batteries contained within a device, you can pack them in your checked bag as long as the device is fully powered off and “protected from accidental activation,” according to the FAA. For devices that generate extreme heat (such as lighters), you must protect the device from switching on inside your checked bag by removing the battery or heating element. Your specific airline may have additional rules regarding lithium batteries. For instance, Southwest has one of the strictest battery policies in the sky: Passengers are limited to one power bank per person, batteries are prohibited in overhead bins and they must be visible while in use. The above guidelines apply only to lithium batteries. “Dry” batteries, such as AAs, button cells and 9-volts, are allowed in both checked and carry-on bags. However, FAA guidelines state that “Battery terminals (usually the ends) must be protected from short circuit (i.e., the terminals must not come in contact with other metal).” You can keep your batteries safe by storing them in their original packaging, a battery case, the battery pocket of a camera bag or a plastic baggy. However, the FAA does not recommend packing rechargeable batteries in their charging unit. Carrying lithium batteries onboard with you won’t prevent them from catching fire, but it will make it easier for flight crews to respond to any incidents. You can do your part by following these guidelines: - If you drop a lithium battery or battery-containing device between the seats, notify a crew member immediately. - Do not charge external lithium batteries or power banks onboard. - Alert the crew if you notice a device overheating, expanding, smoking or burning. - If your device’s battery is damaged or recalled, do not pack it — dispose of it properly and replace it. Baggage regulations can be tricky, but it’s worth paying attention. Passengers who don’t follow the rules can be slapped with serious fines — and, more importantly, they pose a safety hazard to everyone on their flight. Follow the packing tips above to travel safely and stress-free, and check out our other travel safety tips:

item.title: INSTRUCTION: How to have a Rivals staycation this winter
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Once you start watching, it’s hard not to be hooked by Rivals’ tales of love, passion and revenge from the very first episode. If the first part of season two kept us busy as summer approached, it seems like our dark November evenings are about to get an upgrade. The Cotswolds will be having a Rivals winter, so it seems, thanks to the second half of season two of the hit show landing on Disney+ in all its aristo-rural, 80s hedonist glory on 11 November 2026. And while Jilly Cooper’s fictional county of Rutshire might play host to the likes of Rupert Campbell-Black in an era that far pre-dates the region’s current reputation for glossy private members’ clubs and maddening tourist crowds, that original essence – all tweed, dogs and hockey sticks – is still palpable, if you know where to go. What happened in the first half of Rivals season two, and what's next? Warning: spoilers ahead! The first half of season two certainly didn't disappoint when it came to drama, scandal and the occasional extravagant party. We saw Tony Baddingham (David Tennant) return with a vengeance, determined to bring down his rivals at Venturer, while his affair with Maud O'Hara (Victoria Smurfit) threatened to tear both their families apart. Meanwhile, the romantic tension between Rupert Campbell-Black (Alex Hassell) and Taggie O'Hara (Bella Maclean) continued to simmer, and Lizzie Vereker (Katherine Parkinson) finally decided to follow her heart when it came to Freddie Jones (Danny Dyer). But it was the shocking mid-season finale that left viewers reeling, with Lady Monica Baddingham (Claire Rushbrook) tragically killed when a tree fell on her car during a storm, just hours after discovering her husband's infidelity and deciding to leave him. And if the first six episodes gave us plenty of polo matches, lavish garden parties and glorious countryside backdrops, the second half promises a distinctly more wintry affair. According to Disney+, we can expect Bonfire Night celebrations, the glamorous Hampshire Hunt Ball and a rather turbulent Christmas, all while the battle between Tony and Declan O'Hara (Aidan Turner) reaches new heights. Rupert, meanwhile, will be forced to confront his own demons, with his complicated feelings for Taggie still very much unresolved. So, while we're expecting more of the same outrageous behaviour and extravagant country-house gatherings, there's also a whole new season of Rivals-inspired countryside escapades to look forward to. As a Gloucestershire local herself, Cooper based her Rivals characters – and setting – on the very social scene she was surrounded by, as many of her former neighbours have attested. Her own home was in the quiet, picture-book village of Bisley, though it was nearby market town Tetbury that truly inspired the fictional Cotchester where the Rivals gang get up to no good. So if a day out at the polo or a woodland walk with hounds in arms is your thing, there’s plenty of inspiration to be taken from Jilly Cooper’s pages. That being said, it’s not only the Cotswolds that captures the Rivals spirit – be it cosy pubs frequented by country folk or enterprising eateries bringing back 80s classics. Prawn cocktail, anyone? Tetbury’s famed-yet-friendly Beaufort Polo Club was Cooper’s direct inspiration for many of her plotlines (particularly for Polo, the third book in the Rutshire Chronicles series, but also as the basis for her equestrian rogue Rupert Campbell-Black). All are welcome to attend and watch this ancient ball sport in action – and while the main outdoor season runs from May to September, the club also hosts winter arena polo tournaments, with a programme of fixtures running through the colder months. All tournaments are free to watch from the sidelines, apart from the annual Beaufort International, and those keen to try their hand at the sport can book polo lessons throughout the year. Be sure to check the fixture list before visiting. And yes, when the outdoor season returns, you do get to stomp the divots. Address: Downfarm House, Westonbirt, Tetbury GL8 8QW Walk around the Bathurst Estate and Cirencester Park It’s easy to imagine the plummy Lady Monica Baddingham residing on the sprawling Bathurst Estate, dating back to the 1700s and surrounded by beautiful parkland. Here, you can plan a picturesque winter walk – dogs welcome – or horse lovers can explore one of the many riding routes amongst the listed woodland (separate riding passes are required). For those interested in the estate's history, guided walks exploring its Second World War connections are also available on selected dates in November. At the Old Kennels, you’ll find some locally run food spots as well as the familiarly named micro-brewery Corinium Ales – where you can enjoy a pint in the taproom or join one of the brewery's festive events, including a Christmas sing-along in December. A pass is required to enter Cirencester Park, although the Old Kennels is free to visit. Address: Estate Office, Bathurst, Park St, Cirencester GL7 2BU There’s something so quintessentially English about Goodwood, be it the rolling Sussex countryside surrounding it or its fascinating history. Festival of Speed et al aside, the estate could easily facilitate a host of Rivals-adjacent experiences, from Land Rover off-roading to clay shooting. In winter, visitors can also enjoy a crisp countryside walk or, come December, a festive afternoon tea at Goodwood House followed by candlelit Christmas carols outside the historic building. There’s an on-site hotel and cosy cottages with country-chic interiors, too, and a number of farm-to-fork restaurants serving seasonal dishes made with produce from the estate's own farm. Explore the honey-stoned Cotswold villages For a true slice of the Cotswold life lived by the likes of Taggie O’Hara and Sarah Stratton, you’ll need to seek out the quieter villages such as Snowshill, Painswick or Upper Slaughter. All offer great walking routes and a glimpse at the charming cottages and gardens that define the region so deeply – particularly lovely on a crisp winter morning, followed by a cosy pub lunch – though those looking for more to do may prefer to explore one of the busier boltholes such as Broadway or Stow-on-the-Wold – just prepare to join the crowds. Come Christmas, Broadway hosts late-night shopping evenings, complete with twinkling lights, festive food and mulled wine, while Painswick's Rococo Garden transforms into an illuminated wonderland on selected evenings throughout the festive season. Found firmly amongst quintessential Jilly Cooper territory in Tetbury, Calcot Manor & Spa offers ample accommodation choice from playful family rooms to luxurious tree houses complete with woodburners and private saunas on their decks – as well as an inviting spa with a heated indoor pool, sauna, steam room and fireside outdoor hot tub, perfect for warming up after a crisp winter walk through the surrounding countryside (though riotous Rivals–inspired parties are not allowed, sadly). Just around the corner is Highgrove House, King Charles’ beloved country residence, so you’re certainly in good company. Address: Gloucestershire, Tetbury GL8 8YJ There’s no better place to rub shoulders with the polo crowd than Coworth Park, Ascot’s 18th century country house which has had a timeless Dorchester Collection makeover. No matter your suite, there’s a view to behold – whether it’s the estate’s rolling grounds or the on-site polo fields (it’s the only hotel in the UK with its own). While the polo season takes place during the warmer months, winter is a lovely time to explore the estate's 240 acres of countryside on horseback, before retreating to Coworth's chic spa for a dip in the heated indoor pool. Come Christmas, the hotel also hosts festive afternoon teas in The Drawing Room, with carol singers on selected weekends, while The Barn serves up seasonal British classics beside a crackling fire. For Michelin-starred dining and one of the best bread baskets I've ever had in my life, book a table at Woven by Adam Smith. Address: Blacknest Rd, Sunningdale, Ascot SL5 7SE Renting one of the very honey-hued homes reminiscent of Cooper's fictional Rutshire is undoubtedly one of the better ways to experience the Cotswolds, and they don’t come much more Rivals-coded than this. There's a choice of a number of properties from the grand to the quaint, though the historic manor house feels remarkably like O’Hara territory, complete with cosy beamed ceilings and even an outdoor tennis court (should you, ahem, wish to recreate a certain scene from series one). Come winter, there's also a log-burning stove, an open fireplace and a secluded outdoor hot tub to retreat to, while the private cinema room is perfect for a cosy evening in. For something a little more extravagant, guests can arrange private dining, wine tastings or cocktail-making classes – just the sort of indulgence the Rivals crowd would approve of. Address: The Manor, Temple Guiting, Cheltenham GL54 5RP Where to eat and drink for a Rivals winter A Cotswolds pub is a thing of beauty – be it one of many new gastro takeovers appealing to the London crowd or the classic old boozers that still maintain their dependable charm. The Wheatsheaf Inn in Northleach arguably comes somewhere in between, thanks to a menu that strikes a balance between fresh new dishes and hearty classics – not to mention its roaring fires and cosy corners, perfect for settling into after a crisp winter walk. During the festive season, the historic coaching inn also offers festive dining, seasonal drinks and even boutique bedrooms upstairs for those who fancy making a night of it. Address: Wheatsheaf Inn, West End, Northleach, Gloucestershire, GL54 3EZ If Rivals’ nostalgic food sequences have you craving Steak Diane and devilled eggs, you’re not alone. Get your fix at London’s beloved retro spot Oslo Court, where the salmon-toned interiors and ruffle curtains only add to the time capsule feel. From prawn cocktails to melon balls, crudités and melba toast finished off with old-fashioned rice pudding for dessert, Oslo Court nonchalantly sidesteps the rest of the London restaurant scene and remains firmly in a glorious time warp – and crucially, does it very well. With its old-school silver service, generous portions and wonderfully theatrical atmosphere, it's also just the place to settle in for a long, indulgent dinner on a chilly winter evening. A short drive from Beaufort Polo Club you’ll find The Cat & Custard Pot, a local favourite and popular with the post-match polo set. Once a royal favourite (it’s King Charles’ local, and previously frequented by both Prince William and Harry), it’s well-loved for its no-fuss vibes – and come winter, a seat beside the fire with a local pint or a hearty Sunday roast is just the ticket. For something a little different, there's also an Italian Chalet serving pizzas and pasta, with live music on Sunday evenings. Address: The Street, Shipton Moyne, Tetbury, GL8 8PN

item.title: Exploring the UK's surreal, man-made 'Alps'
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
'Unlike anything else in the country': Exploring the UK's surreal 'Alps' The "Cornish Alps" are home to vivid green lagoons and man-made pyramid-shaped peaks. Now, a series of new trails are opening up this vast industrial area to travellers. Clawing at the gravel, I pull myself onto the summit and brush chalky dust from my legs. The wind tugs at my hair as I survey my "kingdom" below. A car appears from the north, speeding towards the village, and I drop to my knees. Pulling back an imaginary bowstring, I take aim and release my arrow towards the passing vehicle before ducking out of sight. It's the late 1990s, and I'm playing with friends on Flatty, one of two towering heaps of china clay waste on the outskirts of St Dennis, the Cornish village where I grew up. Pointy, its conical companion, rises nearby. Together, these surreal snow-white slopes form part of Clay Country, known affectionately by locals as the "Cornish Alps". Here, more than 250 years of mining has transformed a 35-sq-mile (91-sq-km) expanse of small farmsteads and former heath and moorland uplands into a landscape of vast pits, vivid green lagoons and man-made peaks. It's a far cry from the surfy, sandy south-west of England printed on postcards. Today, the Cornish Alps are changing. As old pits close, vegetation is taking over, wildlife is returning and new multi-use trails are opening up areas that have long been off limits. On a recent autumn weekend, I returned home to walk these routes, explore new corners of my hometown and see what's changed as the land is handed back to nature. Cornwall's 'white gold' In 1746, Plymouth chemist William Cookworthy identified a source of china clay, also known as kaolin, near Helston while searching for materials to replicate the porcelain imported from China. Tin miners had long used the heat-resistant clay, known locally as moorstone, to repair cracks in furnaces. Cookworthy recognised its potential for making porcelain, later identifying purer and larger deposits near the town of St Austell. In 1768, Cookworthy patented his formula for hard-paste porcelain. As demand for china clay grew in the 19th Century, mining expanded rapidly around St Austell, transforming the landscape and providing livelihoods for generations of Cornish families. Prized for its commercial value, the clay became known as "white gold" and was used in everyday products from toothpaste to cosmetics. By 1910, Cornwall was producing around 50% of the world's china clay – roughly one million tonnes a year – and exporting about three-quarters of its output. "You could hear the sirens going in your classroom and hear the blasting," recalled Clay Country native Steve Hawken, referring to the industry's mid-20th-Century heyday, when working pits were right outside homes and schools. Today, Hawken works as a volunteer guide at Wheal Martyn, the UK's only china clay museum. Set within two former Victorian-era clay works near St Austell, the museum tells the story of Cornwall's china clay industry and its impact on local life. It also serves as an information point for visitors exploring the nearby Luxulyan Valley and Charlestown areas of the Unesco-inscribed Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape. At 15, Hawken began a 37-year career in the clay mining industry, cycling to nearby Littlejohns Pit to run errands as a "kettle boy". Just beyond the car park, he pointed out the old, water-filled Lansalson Pit. "To go down deep, you have to expand [the pit] wide, or else it gets too dangerous," he explained in a broad Cornish accent. Today, flooded pits like Lansalson are a defining feature of the landscape, their milky turquoise waters reminiscent of the glacial lakes of the Canadian Rockies. But don't be fooled: swimming here is dangerous and strictly forbidden. "It's roughly 50 yards (46m) deep, about the width of a football pitch, but there's probably about 48 yards (44m) of china clay [underneath the surface], which is why it's that colour." Despite its significant contribution to Cornwall's economy and industrial heritage, Clay Country is largely overlooked by tourists. As novelist Daphne du Maurier once wrote: "These hills beyond St Austell, where they work the clay, are unlike anything else in the country." Today, the best way to explore the Alps' industrial heritage is on foot. In 2025, Imerys, the French corporation that owns the land, opened up previously inaccessible areas by adding 21 miles (34km) of footpaths – many also open to cyclists and horse riders – bringing its network to 38 miles (62km). These permissive paths (publicly accessible trails on private land) are scattered around old mining sites, with some linking to the larger Clay Trails that connect to places like Par Beach and Luxulyan Valley along the National Cycle Network. Starting at Wheal Martyn, I traced a five-mile (8km) Clay Trail that begins along an old railway siding where china clay was once loaded onto steam engines bound for Cornwall's Par Docks. Passing gardens with fluttering Cornish flags, I followed waymarkers along sandy tracks, spotting fungi-dotted grass as I neared Carn Grey, a rocky outcrop near the village of Trethurgy. After circling the paths and flooded pits of Pentruff and Baal, I stopped for a sandwich. There's nowhere to buy food along the way, so walkers should do as the Cornish do and pack "crib" (a mid-morning snack). The green scrub and autumnal foliage softened the slopes, and bird calls echoed across the water as several small gulls bobbed on the surface. Plan your visit: The permissive paths and Cornwall's Clay Trails are generally open each day, year-round, and are free to access. Because portions of the path run near the kaolin pits and industrial processing sites, it's important to stay on the marked trails. In the distance, Great Treverbyn Tip, known locally as "Sky Tip", has stood here since the 1930s. For every tonne of clay extracted, up to nine tonnes of waste were left behind, creating at least 100 pale, pyramid-shaped peaks that dominated the skyline. Today, only a few remain. Once considered eyesores, they have become familiar landmarks, framed in the windows of local homes for generations. When Imerys proposed flattening Sky Tip in 2014, residents rallied to save it. Today, Cornwall's flag flies from its summit, a symbol of local pride and victory. Although mining here has declined, there are still decades of china clay reserves to be worked, supporting local jobs and generating an estimated £40m ($53.9m) a year for the local economy. To appreciate the industry's continued importance, I headed up to nearby Caerloggas Downs for sweeping views across St Austell Bay, where, on a clear day, you might spot ships leaving to transport china clay around the globe. The permissive paths crisscrossed the former quarry, and I followed one to the top through patches of purple heather. On the horizon, the Sky Tip's symmetrical silhouette looked entirely out of place, like an ancient monument transplanted to the Cornish coast. I continued back along the Clay Trail, through quiet woodland until I reached Trethurgy, where a single raincloud in an otherwise blue sky followed me to my final destination: Bodelva Pit, one of the area's most ambitious transformations. Its iron-rich clay was once used to produce the Financial Times' iconic pink paper. Today, it's home to the renowned Eden Project, with its vast indoor rainforest and 30 acres of gardens. Elsewhere in Clay Country, the former kaolin pit at Dubbers, near the village of Nanpean, has also been returned to nature since closing in the 1960s. In late 2024, more than 100,000 native trees were planted in one of south-west England's largest tree-planting schemes. Today, up to four miles (6.4km) of new permissive paths wind through thriving woodland and heathland, home to red deer, dormice and birds including jack snipe and little ringed plover. Another day, I walked over to meet Molly Earl, who runs Bees Off, which rescues honeybee colonies from chimneys and other structures before rehoming them at sites such as Dubbers. "They're quite calm today," she said, handing me a protective hooded jacket and examining one of her 35 hives. She explained that come spring, the bees feast on gorse, heather, clover and other wildflowers. "You've got to have [the hives] in an area where they're going to get loads of different pollens," Earl said. "I could write you a list that would stretch from your head to your toes of all the things around here." Our conversation turned to our childhoods and how radically the landscape has changed. "Nature always finds a way," she smiled. It got me thinking about one place I hadn't yet revisited: Flatty and Pointy. Walking back towards St Dennis, I realised how sentimental I was about these two old tips. To the kids of Clay Country, they were our wild, unruly playgrounds. As we grew older, they became markers of home, familiar shapes we search for while driving along the A30. Standing between them, they seemed smaller than I remembered. When people ask where I'm from, I often say, "near Newquay", a place they're more likely to recognise. But reflecting on the past few days, I've come to appreciate how much this corner of Cornwall has shaped the county. Perhaps it's time I stopped giving the easy answer. From now on, I'll proudly say I'm from the Cornish Alps. – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: REVIEW: Is Frontier's Business Bundle worth the extra miles? I put it to the test
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Can a low-cost carrier ever really be premium? Frontier Airlines certainly seems to think so. In recent years, the airline has added front-of-plane seating with extra legroom and blocked middle seats, combined its extras into fare bundles and even announced plans for first class. You can pay for those bundles with Frontier Miles, too. The top-tier Business Bundle is the closest thing Frontier has to a premium experience, with just about every bell and whistle the airline offers. The catch? It usually costs more than double the miles of a bare-bones Basic fare. Are the extra miles worth it? I put it to the test by taking one flight on a Basic fare, then another on the Business Bundle. What are Frontier's fare bundles? Frontier sells a no-frills Basic fare plus three bundles that add bags, seats and flexibility, and you can book any of them with cash or miles. The amounts below are minimum one-way prices per traveler. Taxes and fees start at $5.60, and miles can only be redeemed for a bundle at the time of the original booking. - Basic: One personal item only. Carry-on bags, checked bags, and seat selection all cost extra. Frontier Miles members generally board in Group 5 unless they qualify for an earlier group, while remaining Basic-fare passengers board in Groups 6 or 7. Award flights start from 5,000 miles plus $5.60 in taxes and fees. - Economy Bundle: Also includes a carry-on bag, a standard seat assignment and no change or cancellation fees. Frontier Miles members board in Group 2 (everyone else on this bundle boards in Group 3). Award flights start from 7,000 miles. - Premium Bundle: Everything in the Economy Bundle, plus a premium seat with extra legroom and Group 1 boarding. Award flights start from 9,000 miles. - Business Bundle: Everything in the Premium Bundle, plus two checked bags of up to 50 pounds each and an UpFront Plus seat at the front of the plane, with either a guaranteed empty middle seat next to you or a larger 2-2 seat (once they enter service). Award flights start from 13,000 miles. My first Frontier flight was from St. Louis Lambert International Airport (STL) to Denver International Airport (DEN). I paid for it with the 5,000 miles I'd earned from Frontier Airlines' Super Bowl promotion earlier this year (offer no longer available), so only the $5.60 in taxes and fees came out of my pocket. Transferring Rove miles to Frontier is also an easy way to top up your balance. You really can't argue with that value for a two-hour flight. The trade-off, as anyone who's flown a low-cost carrier will know, is everything you don't get. A Basic fare only covers a personal item. That turned out to be the biggest frustration of my Frontier experience, as this won't be a realistic option for folks traveling for longer than a day or two. Boarding in Group 5 as a Frontier Miles member wasn't an issue, and the process was more orderly and civilized than I expected. With nothing to put in the overhead bins, there wasn't a need to board early anyway. I just found my seat all the way back in row 27 (I couldn't select it myself) and settled in. The flight itself was uneventful and punctual, which on a low-cost airline is really about all you can ask for. For my second flight, a short hop from Denver to Kansas City International Airport (MCI), I booked the Business Bundle, and the perks landed before I even got to the airport. Being able to select Seat 1A during booking sure was convenient. True to the UpFront Plus promise, the seat next to me was empty. Frontier's new 2-2 first-class seats had not yet entered service when I flew, so my aircraft retained the existing 3-3 layout. I boarded in Group 1, right behind preboarding, and didn't need to pay extra for luggage. The bundle included a full-size carry-on and two checked bags, each weighing up to 50 pounds, which was far more than I needed for this short trip. What you won't get, in any bundle, is complimentary food or drinks. Frontier doesn't include food, drinks or lounge access with its bundles, so anything you want on board comes at an extra cost, and it was a sobering reminder that this was still a low-cost carrier. Is it worth redeeming more miles for a Business Bundle on Frontier? Unless I needed to pack a lot of luggage or particularly valued the extra space of an UpFront Plus seat, I don't think I'd spring for a Business Bundle again, whether I was paying with cash or redeeming Frontier miles. For even the cheapest redemptions, the Business Bundle costs 8,000 more miles than a Basic fare, which is more than double the price. For a short domestic flight with nothing to eat or drink, that's a lot more miles. Frontier's Business Bundle is not a bad product. It's just that a Basic fare for as little as 5,000 miles at that price is terrific value, and that's a tough act to follow. For most travelers, the sweet spot is probably the Economy Bundle. It starts at just 2,000 more miles than a Basic fare and fixes the thing I missed most on my first flight, a proper carry-on, while making your booking far more flexible. I'd be happy with that for my next Frontier flight. So, can a low-cost carrier be premium? After flying both fares back-to-back, the Business Bundle felt more like paying for convenience, baggage and personal space than a genuinely premium experience. Your own experience will depend a lot on the route, the dates and how much luggage you need to take, and Frontier's lowest award rates won't always be available. Unless you need two checked bags or place a high value on the extra space of an UpFront Plus seat, the Economy Bundle is probably the better balance of price and useful benefits.
